en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai taught that the practice of the holy ones regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is briefly threefold: first, worldly meditation; second, world-transcending meditation; and third, the supreme meditation.
Worldly meditation is further divided into two: first, the fundamental "tasting" meditation (*āsvādana-dhyāna*), which is obscured, defiled, and...
[This is] the record.
Second, the fundamental pure dhyāna:
it is non-obscured, stainless, and determinate.
The "Root" refers to the foundation of both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas' attainment of the Way, their turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and their entry into Nirvana all occur within dhyāna."
If one can deeply contemplate the fundamental [state], giving rise to the most excellent and sublime higher absorption (samādhi), it is therefore called "fundamental.
As for "disappearing," it refers to realizing through darkness, lacking the wisdom of contemplation (vipaśyanā).
That which is "with defilement" refers to the arising of attachment to the flavor [of meditative experience] in each stage.
That which is "indeterminate" refers to the lack of clarity regarding the object.
This has three grades:
This refers to dhyāna, samādhi, and śūnyatā;
that is, the twelve gates of dhyāna.

When first practicing the preparatory methods, one should skillfully distinguish between wind and labored breathing, clearly recognize the correct breath, and calmly and slowly count it, ensuring there is no increase or decrease.
If one counts with subtlety, skillfully understands the shifting of objects, and achieves equilibrium, one shall realize the preliminary methods (*sāmantaka-dharma*).

Whether in coarse or subtle abiding, there arises the method of sustaining the body (*kāyadhāraṇa-dharma*), whereby one advances to attain the concentration of desire (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
When the eight contacts are activated and the five factors are perfected, this is the arising of the first dhyāna.
The *Mahā-śāstra* says:
"Having already attained freedom from the fire of lust, one then obtains the cool, refreshing concentration."
"It is like a person suffering from great heat who finds joy upon entering a cool pool," and so forth.

If one wishes to advance upward and depart from the lower realms, ordinary persons rely on the contemplation of the six practices (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-bhāvanā*), while the disciples of the Buddha mostly cultivate the eight noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

In the factors of initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) within the first dhyāna, the practitioner develops weariness toward and detachment from initial application and sustained application, regarding the first dhyāna as suffering.
These two factors—coarseness (*audārika*) and hindrance (*āvaraṇa*)—are suffering because they disturb the concentrated mind;
they are coarse because the joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) arise from them.
The two factors—the obscuration and the superior concentration—are obstacles.
The second dhyāna differs from this and is therefore termed "superior," "sublime," and "transcendent.

In summary, first, knowing the faults and not being attached; second, reproaching them; and third, analyzing and breaking them down—to thus attain detachment from the first dhyāna is the characteristic of cultivating the second dhyāna.
When one skillfully clings to disenchantment, then both internally and externally become luminously clear; this arises together with joy, and the four factors are accomplished.
Thus, the *Śāstra* says:

"Therefore, by abandoning applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one enters the sphere of a single consciousness (*ekajñānāyatana*); because the internal mind is pure, joy and bliss born of concentration are attained," and so forth.
In the second dhyāna, since one has already abandoned applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one cannot employ preparatory means (*upāya*).

When emerging from meditative absorption, one practices the cultivation of revulsion toward the lower stage and progress toward the higher; this also involves six aspects, as described in the methods for relinquishing the first dhyāna, and so forth.
At that time, one becomes utterly absorbed, no longer relying on either the internal or the external; bliss arises simultaneously, and the five factors are perfected.
Thus, the *Śāstra* says: "From craving comes suffering;
when joy is lost, sorrow arises. When one is free from both suffering and pleasure, the body is at ease; [this is] equanimity, mindfulness, and skillful means," and so forth.
Desiring to weary of the lower stage and advance to the higher, there are likewise six modes of practice, as previously detailed at length.

Through skillful cultivation, the mind opens wide and becomes luminous; inhalation and exhalation cease, and [the mind] arises together with equanimity (*upekṣā*). It is empty, radiant, and tranquil, thus accomplishing the four factors.
"If one can know the affliction inherent in pleasure and perceive the great security of the immovable,
sorrow and joy have already been eliminated, and suffering and happiness are now also severed," and so forth.
Once the practitioner has internally realized the four dhyānas, if they wish to externally cultivate merit and virtue, they should study the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
This [cultivation] includes both general cultivation and specific cultivation.
Regarding general cultivation, the *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"This loving-kindness is cultivated within the four dhyānas of the form realm."
This statement is general.
As for specific cultivation: since the first dhyāna possesses vitarka and vicāra, it is easy to cultivate compassion;
because the factor of joy (prīti) is present, it is easy to cultivate sympathetic joy (muditā).
It is easy to cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) through the factor of joy;
it is easy to cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*) through the factor of one-pointedness of mind.
Furthermore, it is easy to cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*) in the first dhyāna.
It is easy to cultivate joy in the second dhyāna;
it is easy to cultivate loving-kindness in the third dhyāna;
it is easy to cultivate equanimity in the fourth dhyāna.
This is the locus for cultivating the four immeasurable concentrations (*apramāṇa-samādhi*).
Furthermore, at the time of cultivation, one enters meditative absorption by taking as an object the signs of joy and equanimity regarding others' freedom from suffering and attainment of happiness.
At the time of its arising, one internally attains the dharma of equanimity regarding joy and bliss, while externally seeing the person before one leave suffering and attain happiness;
or one may internally attain it while not seeing it externally, or see it externally while not attaining it internally—thus distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, and so forth.
The practitioner who wishes to transcend the cage of form cultivates the four formless absorptions (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*).
By extinguishing form and preserving the mind, with each moment of mind depending upon the next, they are called the "four formless [absorptions].
As for the skillful means (*upāya*), one must reprove that form is the root of suffering; hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—form is a mass of suffering.

He praises emptiness as pure and sublime, free from all oppression, transcending all form, and corresponding with the meditative absorption of emptiness; this state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure increases further and further.
Within deep meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one perceives only empty space, devoid of all material forms, and the mind is without distraction.
Furthermore, because one has attained the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one transcends the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); therefore, it is called "transcending all signs of form.
Because the mind is sustained by the dharma of emptiness, various material forms cannot arise; therefore, it is called "extinguishing the signs of resistance (*sapratigha-lakṣaṇa*)."

Having attained the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one is definitively able to relinquish material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) because one no longer recollects or yearns for them; thus it is said, "not dwelling on various marks of form," and so forth.
Both the disparagement of lower realms and the ascent to higher ones possess their respective skillful means, as detailed at length in the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Dhyāna), and so forth.
The fundamental *sāsvāda-dhyāna* (tasting dhyāna) is concluded.
The fundamental *śuddha-dhyāna* (pure dhyāna) is non-obscured, stainless, and determinate; it is the opposite of the aforementioned [defiled states].
This, moreover, consists of three categories: namely, the Six Sublime Gates (*ṣaḍ-āyatana-mukha*), the Sixteen Special Victories (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*), and the Universal Clarity (*sarva-prakāśa*), etc.
Nirvana is sublime, and these six can lead to it; therefore, they are called the "Six Sublime Gates.

These three dharmas constitute the nature of the three roots; for those in whom the nature of wisdom predominates, the Six Sublime Gates are taught. Each of these gates is capable of giving rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava) state even within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
If those whose natures are predominantly characterized by concentration (*samādhi*), one teaches them the Sixteen Superior Stages (*ṣoḍaśābhivijñāna*).
Therefore, the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state does not arise in the lower stages; only when the dhyānas of the higher stages are perfected can one attain awakening.
For those whose natures are equal in concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*), one teaches the Universal Clarities (*sāmānyābhijñā*).
The wisdom of the clear observation (*vipaśyanā*) of the *abhijñās* is profound and subtle; from the lower stages to the upper, it is capable of giving rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.

This is an explanation given according to the capacities of beings; if one were to treat this as an application of specific remedies (*pratipakṣa*), there would be further distinct paths, and so forth.
If one were to explain the cultivation in detail, it would encompass all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
For now, however, we shall merely follow the sequential arising [of the stages], maintaining a single consistent line of thought.
When these six gates are cultivated and discussed together with their realization, there are twelve factors.
The Buddha said:
"Abiding and moving in three and four gives rise to twelve.
This refers to the cultivation and realization of the factors of mindfulness, up to the cultivation and realization of the factors of purity.

Regarding the cultivation of counting: the practitioner first harmonizes the breath so that it is neither constricted nor slippery, then calmly and slowly counts from one to ten. They focus the mind upon the counting and do not allow it to wander or scatter; this is called the cultivation of counting.

Regarding "corresponding with the count": the awakened mind proceeds spontaneously from one to ten without the application of effort; the mind abides naturally in the count, the breath becomes subtle and the mind refined—this is called "realizing the count."
If one suffers from excessive coarseness in counting, one should let go of counting and cultivate following; this applies likewise up to the stage of purity.
Furthermore, there are three meanings of "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*):
first, the contemplation of reality through wisdom (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*).
2. Attaining the contemplation of understanding, which is the contemplation of mental imagery;
3. The contemplation of reality.
Among these, one first employs the contemplation of reality and subsequently employs the contemplation of wisdom.

One who cultivates the contemplation of reality, within a state of meditative concentration, uses the eye of the mind to clearly observe this body: the subtle characteristics of inhalation and exhalation are like the wind in the sky;
the thirty-six components—skin, flesh, sinews, and bones—are as unsubstantial as a plantain tree, impure both internally and externally, and utterly loathsome.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the feelings of joy, bliss, and so forth within meditative concentration all possess the characteristic of disintegration; they are suffering and not pleasure.
Moreover, one contemplates that within meditative concentration, the mental consciousness is impermanent, not abiding for even a single moment, and has no place to which it can cling.

Furthermore, one contemplates that within meditative concentration, all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are entirely subject to causes and conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
When contemplating in this manner, one can destroy the four inversions;
since a self or person cannot be found, what could concentration possibly depend upon?
This is called the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
When practicing in this way, one perceives the inhalation and exhalation of the breath pervading all the pores.

The mind’s eye opens and becomes clear, penetratingly seeing the thirty-six internal constituents within the body, as well as the various openings for parasites—the impurity both internal and external.
Oppressed by manifold sufferings and subject to momentary change,
all phenomena are seen to be entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
The mind gives rise to both sorrow and joy, having nothing upon which to rely.
One attains the four foundations of mindfulness and shatters the four inversions.
This is called being in accord with contemplation; it would be impossible to record all such details in full.
The Buddha sat beneath a tree and inwardly contemplated *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), such as the stages of counting and following; this is precisely this dhyāna.
Regarding the "Sixteen Superiorities" (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*), the explanation of their names is as follows [and so forth].
This is named according to its causes and conditions. Regarding the cultivation of the signs:

"knowing the inhalation and knowing the exhalation" refers to counting the breaths as a substitute for the practice of *ānāpānasmṛti*. One regulates the breath so that it becomes subtle and fine, following the breath with a single mind. When inhaling, one knows it from the nose to the navel; when exhaling, one knows it from the navel to the nose, observing it continuously without distraction.
One knows that wind, panting, and breath are coarse;
one knows that the inhalation is subtle.
When the coarse enters, one immediately regulates it to make it subtle, like a gatekeeper who knows both entry and exit, blocking the evil and allowing the good to proceed.
One knows roughness and smoothness, lightness and heaviness, cold and warmth, duration and proximity, and difficulty and ease.
One knows that the breath is the support of life; if even a single breath does not return, life immediately ends.
One awakens to the fact that breath and life are precarious and impermanent, and thus does not give rise to craving or pride.
Knowing that the breath is not the self, one does not give rise to views.
If one knows the length of the breath, it corresponds to the concentration of the desire realm.
Knowing the breath pervading the entire body corresponds to the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*).
Eliminating all bodily formations corresponds to the factors of initial application and sustained application (*vitarka-vicāra*) in the first dhyāna;
experiencing joy corresponds to the factor of joy (*prīti*).
The experience of pleasure corresponds to the factor of joy;
the experience of mental formations corresponds to the factor of one-pointedness of mind.
When the mind produces gladness, it is dhyāna accompanied by joy.
The mind’s application of concentration is the factor of one-pointedness of mind in the second dhyāna;
the mind’s application of liberation is the bliss of the third dhyāna;
and the contemplation of impermanence is the immovability of the fourth dhyāna.
Contemplating emergence and dispersion is the sphere of infinite space;
contemplating detachment from desire is the sphere of infinite consciousness;
contemplating cessation corresponds to the sphere of nothingness.
Regarding the contemplation of relinquishment (*upekṣā*), it corresponds to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
When one contemplates relinquishment, one immediately attains the *nirvāṇa* of the three vehicles.
If one discusses the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*) in a horizontal sense, it corresponds to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and so forth.
Regarding the dhyāna of universal clarity (*sāmānyābhijñā-dhyāna*), the practitioner contemplates the three things—breath, form, and mind—as being without distinction.
He observes the inhalation and exhalation with precise discernment: the inhalation does not accumulate, and the exhalation does not disperse;
it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, like wind in space, its nature being non-existent.
Breath fundamentally depends upon the body, yet the body fundamentally does not exist.
The deluded thoughts of past lives have summoned the present four great elements (mahābhūta), which enclose empty space; this is conventionally designated as the "body.
Its six parts, such as the head, its thirty-six components, and each of the four subtle elements (tanmātra), are individually not the body.
Contemplate that the body arises from the mind, and the mind arises from conditions; their arising and ceasing are so rapid that no abiding place or characteristic can be seen.
There is only a name, yet even the name is empty.
Thus, when one contemplates the breath, form, and mind, one does not find any distinct difference between these three natures.
Since one does not find these three things, one does not find any phenomena at all; this is the characteristic of cultivation.
As for "realization," it refers to internally realizing the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which is empty and corresponds to one's contemplative understanding.

One sequentially penetrates this body, clearly discerning its physical form and breath; one also understands that the celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography of the world correspond to the body. One is able to possess the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) of the three realms and recognize that even in the realm of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti), there exist subtle afflictions. By destroying these delusions and giving rise to the truth, one attains the nirvāṇa of the Three Vehicles.
All [of these] are contained within the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Dhyāna).
This concludes the mundane dhyāna.
Second, to clarify supramundane dhyāna, there are four types, namely: contemplation (*guan*), refinement (*lian*), perfuming (*xun*), and cultivation (*xiu*).

"Contemplation" refers to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*); these are collectively termed "contemplative dhyāna.
To extinguish the fire of lust, the practitioner must necessarily cultivate these notions until they are thoroughly matured.
At whatever time one contemplates, it is in conjunction with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Holding the mind through the perception of form, the mind is not distracted; one is thus able to eliminate worldly craving and destroy the six types of desire:

attachment to colors such as red, white, yellow, or black; attachment to physical beauty; attachment to dignified demeanor and graceful gestures; attachment to charming speech; attachment to smooth and delicate skin; or attachment to a person who is pleasing to the mind.
This abyss of the six desires submerges practitioners.
One who can cultivate the nine contemplations will eliminate these six thieves:
the contemplation of death destroys both the desire for dignified demeanor and the desire for speech.
The perception of bloating, the perception of decay, and the perception of being devoured destroy the desire for physical form.
The perception of being smeared with blood, the perception of bluish discoloration, and the perception of festering pus destroy the desire for color.
The contemplation of the skeleton and the contemplation of burning eliminate the desire for physical delicacy.
The nine contemplations collectively eliminate the desire for persons to whom one is attached.
Furthermore, the contemplation of being devoured and the contemplation of disintegration eliminate attachment to persons as objects of the mind.
Since these nine [stages] eliminate desire and also attenuate hatred and delusion, the mountain of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is shaken.
Although this is but the initial gateway of impurity (*aśubha*), it is capable of accomplishing great matters.
It is like a corpse in the sea; by relying upon it, one is able to cross over, and so forth.
Regarding the names of the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*):
they are called "liberations" because one turns one's back on the five pure sensual desires and abandons the mind of attachment.

As for cultivation: the practitioner maintains pure precepts and makes great vows, desiring to accomplish the great task; with body upright and mind rectified, they clearly observe the big toe of the foot, visualizing it as being like a black, swollen, and protruding soybean.
When this visualization is accomplished, one further advances it until it is the size of a wild bean,
then the size of a finger,
and then the size of a chicken egg.
Next, one observes the second, third, fourth, and fifth fingers.
Then one contemplates the sole of the foot, the heel, the ankle, the instep, the knee, the thigh, and the hip, seeing them all as swollen.
Next, observe the right foot in the same manner.
Furthermore, one should visualize the passages for excrement and urine, the waist, spine, abdomen, back, chest, and ribs, all appearing swollen.
Furthermore, one contemplates the right shoulder blade, arm, elbow, wrist, palm, and five fingers, as well as the head, jaw, and so forth.
From the feet to the head, and from the head to the feet, one observes the body in its entirety; seeing nothing but swelling, a sense of revulsion arises in the mind.
Furthermore, one should contemplate decay and putrefaction:
from the passages for feces and urine, pus and worms flow out, more foul-smelling than a dead dog.
Since one's own body is thus, one should observe that those whom one loves are likewise so.
Internally, one destroys the view of self; externally, one destroys craving. Dwelling long in contemplation, one eliminates worldly craving and attachment.
Next, having removed the skin and flesh, one clearly contemplates the white bones.
One observes that the colors and characteristics of the bones differ—namely blue, yellow, white, and pigeon-colored—and likewise, these skeletal characteristics are also devoid of self.
When this contemplation is attained, it is called the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
Next, when observing the bones as blue, one sees this great earth—east, west, south, and north—all appearing entirely blue;
the same is true for yellow, white, and pigeon-colored [bones].
This is the sign of the "not-yet-arrived" stage (*anāgamya*).

Furthermore, when one contemplates the skeletal figure and light issues from between its eyebrows, and within that light one beholds the Buddha, this is the sign of the accomplishment of the first liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Following this sequence, up to the signs of the arising of the eighth liberation, they are fully detailed as described in the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Dhyāna), and so forth.
Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): the first two bases of mastery are situated in the first dhyāna;
the third and fourth bases of mastery are situated in the second dhyāna;
and the final four bases of mastery are situated in the fourth dhyāna.
In the third dhyāna, pleasure is predominant and the mind is dull; therefore, it is not established [as a stage of mastery].

Regarding the previous liberations (vimokṣa), one lacks mastery over the extent of the objects of focus; for this reason, the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) involve even more subtle observation of the few and the many, the beautiful and the ugly, so that one may attain superior knowledge and superior vision of them all—just as a swift horse can both break through an array and also control itself, and so forth.

Regarding the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*): by means of eight forms and two minds, they mutually dissolve into one another, becoming vast, pervasive, and all-encompassing, transforming without obstruction, as described in detail in the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Meditation), and so forth.
The "cultivation of dhyāna" refers to the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*).
Although one has previously attained the eight dhyānas, there were still intervals in their entry.

Now, desiring to bring them to full maturity, one proceeds from the initial shallow stages to the ultimate deep stages, entering them in succession. Because there are no defilements, impurities, or interruptions in between, and because that which was not sequential is now made sequential, they are called "successive."
Furthermore, it is called "refined dhyāna" (*bhāvanā-dhyāna*) because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), refines the tainted (*sāsrava*), and eliminates all intermediate coarseness.
It also refers to the harmonizing of all dhyānas, ensuring that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced and uninterrupted.
The *Abhidharma* clarifies "perfuming and refining," stating only that one perfumes the four dhyānas with the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Now, by universally refining the eight stages with the untainted, this is precisely the sequential entry into the *ānantarya-samādhi*.
The "perfuming dhyāna" (xūn chán) is precisely the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s-leaping samādhi).

The former involves entering sequentially and without interval; this one likewise involves entering sequentially and without interval, and is also able to emerge sequentially and without interval, thereby eliminating coarse intervals as well as the flavors of attachment to dharmas and sensory objects.
It is like a lion, which can both retreat and advance, shaking off all dust and dirt.

When the practitioner enters and emerges from this dharma, it can thoroughly permeate all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), rendering them entirely proficient and allowing for mastery in transformation, just as one might perfume leather until it is supple and then fashion it into objects according to one's will.
The practitioner of dhyāna transcends samādhi.

By transcending into it from near and far, transcending out of it from near and far, and abiding in transcendence from near and far, the merit of this dhyāna is most profound; therefore, it is called "Crest Dhyāna" (mūrdha-dhyāna).
He enters and exits with mastery all the various dharma-gates, and so forth.
Furthermore, he skillfully enters the nine successive attainments and the eight liberations;
he skillfully emerges from the eight liberations with supernormal agility.
This refers to the very same intent: transcending the eight liberations with perfect stability, and skillfully entering, emerging from, and abiding in hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
It is like a painter who, by blending five primary colors, produces an infinite variety of hues.
Just as worldly fruits arise from the four great elements alone to produce all five aggregates, so too is the dharma of meditative concentration:
through contemplation, refinement, perfuming, and cultivation alone, it gives rise to all supernatural powers and transformations, lacking no seed whatsoever.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"A Bodhisattva dwelling in dhyāna attains the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
A stage (*bhūmi*) is able to sustain and able to give birth.
Within each and every dhyāna, there are fully present all practices such as loving-kindness and compassion, vows, the factors of enlightenment, and the six perfections.
Why is this? If one clearly contemplates wisdom within the context of ethical discipline and meditative concentration, this is precisely the application of mindfulness.
To discuss contemplation (vipaśyanā) alone, it is the foundation of mindfulness of nature (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna);
to take universally the objects of morality (śīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā), letters, and so forth, it is the foundation of mindfulness of objects (ālambanasmṛtyupasthāna).
Furthermore, the contemplation of impurity (aśubhabhāvanā), which destroys the inversion of purity, is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).

Contemplating within the various dhyānas that the mind experiences suffering and pleasure, and that such feelings cannot be apprehended internally or externally across the three periods of time, one thereby destroys the inversion of regarding [feeling] as pleasant; this is the application of mindfulness to feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna).

Contemplating the minds within the various dhyānas, one sees that because there is a mind, one performs good and evil deeds, whereas where there is no mind, there is no agent; thus destroying the inversion of regarding [the self] as a permanent entity, this is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna).

Contemplating the arising and ceasing of the mind, one sees that its prior and subsequent limits are severed, thereby destroying the inversion of regarding [existence] as eternal; this is the application of mindfulness to the mind (citta-smṛtyupasthāna).

Furthermore, there are the four foundations of mindfulness through the eight liberations, the refinement of the four foundations of mindfulness through the nine successive attainments, the vigorous cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, and the transcendent cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness.

The followers of the Two Vehicles cultivate these five dhyānas for their own liberation; they achieve the four "withered" foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and do not name this the Stage of Endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).

The Bodhisattva, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, deeply contemplates the foundations of mindfulness with vows of compassion and pity, bearing the burden of all beings and achieving the four "flourishing" foundations of mindfulness; this is the Mahāyāna, named the Stage of Endurance.
Question:
Since there is no form and no body in the formless realm, how can one possess the four foundations of mindfulness?
Answer:
The *Abhidharma* states:
"In the formless realm, there is the morality coexistent with the path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*).

Since this morality consists of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and its objects are pervasive throughout the untainted (*anāsrava*), this moral matter follows the untainted state up to the formless realm."
The author of the *Abhidharmakośa* says:
"Form is a non-instructional dharma (*anupadeśadharma*) and does not reach the formless realm.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma* says:
"Formless yet possessing form.
One should know that the meaning elucidated in the Hinayana contains two aspects.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"The form of the formless realm is not known by the śrāvakas.
If that is so, what harm is there in the four foundations of mindfulness also extending to the formless realm?
Question:

Question: Among the various dhyānas, if one has only attained the clear foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and still lacks the right efforts (samyakpradhāna), how can one possess the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma)?
Answer:
Speaking in terms of the stages (bhūmi), the foundations of mindfulness do not include the subsequent factors.
Cultivation is for the sake of meaning; the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) comprise the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When first cultivating wholesome, out-flowing (sāsrava) aggregates, one attains right mindfulness within conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma); this is precisely the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness."
The four kinds of diligence are precisely right effort (*samyakpradhāna*).
When cultivated within a concentrated mind, they are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
When the five wholesome faculties arise, they are called the faculties (*indriya*).
The growth of the faculties is called "powers.
The discernment of the function of the path is called the "seven factors of enlightenment.
Proceeding securely along the path is called the "eightfold noble path."

If these [factors] are already fully present within the wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava*) at the initial stage, why must the Eightfold Path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*) wait until the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) to exist?

If the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) already possess the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the same logic applies to the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), and so forth.
Just as it is with the contemplation of dhyāna, so it is with its refinement (*tanu*), perfuming (*vāsanā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, within each and every dhyāna, the Bodhisattva, in accordance with the Dharma-gates he enters, regards all sentient beings with compassion, just as parents who have obtained food do not forget their children.

Compassion arises for those who, out of pity for their deluded darkness, do not seek happiness from within themselves but seek it from external others; who are addicted to and mired in the five desires, seeking suffering, gaining fear, and losing joy; and for whom all desires are devoid of true pleasure. It is for them that this compassion is aroused.
Now, since the afflictions are thus, how can one eliminate them?
By attaining the bliss of dhyāna-samādhi, one is no longer deceived by them; for this reason, one arouses loving-kindness.
There are the four great vows.

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the six perfections within the various dhyānas: sentient beings are bound and attached to the world, unable to relinquish their worldly affairs and livelihoods even for a moment.
The Bodhisattva abandons these and enters dhyāna with a single mind; this is called *dāna*.
If one does not maintain the precepts, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) will not arise.
Furthermore, when entering *dhyāna*, the non-arising of discursive thoughts and the spontaneous absence of evil constitute *śīla* (precept).
Restraining body and speech, enduring toil and suffering, preventing external sense objects from attaching, and suppressing internal sense bases from arising—this is *kṣānti* (patience).

During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one maintains continuous mindfulness; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the mind remains constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without the arising of intervening thoughts—this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
With the mind single-pointedly settled in concentration, neither distracted nor attached to its flavor, this is called concentration (*samādhi*).

If one’s mind is single-pointedly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such that one can know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena and deeply recognize what is false and deceptive, this is called *prajñā*.
All various practices are fully perfected within *dhyāna*; within each and every state of *dhyāna*, one can generate all meritorious virtues and bear the burden of compassion.
For this reason, it is named the Land of Endurance (*Kṣānti-bhūmi*).
Third, regarding the supramundane, supreme dhyāna: this refers to the nine kinds of great dhyānas as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*; they will not be discussed in detail here.
The dhyāna of intrinsic nature consists in contemplating the true nature of the mind; it is called the supreme concentration (*adhyāna*).
Among all phenomena, are there any that do not arise from the mind? The mind encompasses everything, just like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
These nine great dhyānas are all the Dharma-realm.
In every state of meditative absorption, the engagement with objects is itself the truth; in every form and every fragrance, there is nothing that is not the Middle Way.
Those of the Two Vehicles do not even know the names of these meditations, much less realize their concentration!

The fundamental, original dhyāna is like milk; refined dhyāna is like curd; perfumed dhyāna is like fresh ghee; cultivated dhyāna is like matured ghee; and the nine great dhyānas are like clarified butter (himalaya). Clarified butter is the most sublime.
Furthermore, when one cultivates the fundamental dhyānas within a mind that relishes their flavor, they become milk;
when cultivated within a mind seeking self-deliverance, they become curd;
and when cultivated within a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, they become fresh butter.
Cultivating within the mind of compassion constitutes the stage of clarified butter (*sarpis*);
cultivating within the mind of ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) constitutes the stage of *ghṛta*;
the other four flavors are likewise. If one does not cultivate with the mind of ultimate reality, they are all termed "coarse."
If one distinguishes between the coarse and the subtle, then ānāpāna is itself the Mahāyāna.
The true reality of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) encompasses all phenomena; beyond this, there is no other excellence.
Therefore, one should know that the Buddhas’ attainment of enlightenment, turning of the wheel of Dharma, and entry into nirvana all occur within the four dhyānas.
To perceive the true reality within the four dhyānas is called the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā); how much more so for other concentrations!
This is precisely the wondrous meaning that transcends all dependencies.
The noble practice of concentration is thus completed.
As for the noble practice of wisdom, it refers to the fourfold wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths, and so forth.

Regarding the wisdom of the Four Truths concerning arising and ceasing: one again contemplates the nine meditations on repulsiveness (*navasaṃjñā*) and the stages of liberation (*vimokṣa*), as well as the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—such as the impure forms of bloating and putrefaction. These are the characteristics of oppression, the characteristics of manifestation, and the characteristics of the three sufferings; this is the wisdom of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

By failing to give rise to non-attachment toward the provisional and the ultimate, one becomes a slave to affection and craving, moving body and speech to produce the three grades of the ten unwholesome karmas. This brings about rebirth in the three miserable realms and the growth of the characteristics of birth, the characteristics of transformation, and the characteristics of the twenty-five states of existence.
Furthermore, one understands the causes and effects of the world, its impurity, and its faults, feeling deep shame, weariness, and abhorrence.

One never kills others to sustain oneself, nor does one seize the bodies of others to fatten one's own; one does not indulge in impurity, nor seek straightness through crookedness; one does not alienate the friendly or unite the hostile, nor mediate between honor and disgrace; one does not practice internal flattery and external sycophancy, nor receive guests without moderation; one does not release poison to harm the Way, nor deviate from the truth through perversity.

Not performing impure deeds or the ten unwholesome actions, but feeling shame and modesty while practicing the three grades of the ten wholesome actions, one brings about birth in the three good realms; this is also the characteristic of growth, the characteristic of transformation, and the characteristic of the twenty-five states of existence.
This is called the wisdom regarding the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
By contemplating the impurity of the basis and its objects, one destroys the inversion of purity;
by contemplating all sensations (*vedanā*) as being the three types of suffering, one destroys the inversion of pleasure.
Contemplating the harmony of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) breaks the inversion of self;
contemplating the arising and ceasing of all mental states breaks the inversion of permanence.

Through specific and general characteristics, skillful right effort, the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*), one proceeds toward the gateway to *nirvāṇa*.
Compassion, vows, the six perfections, and various practices are the characteristics of the Mahāyāna.

They are also the characteristics of morality, concentration, and wisdom; they are also the characteristics of that which can eliminate [afflictions]. This is called the wisdom of the Truth of the Path.
When inversion does not arise, karma does not arise;
when karma does not arise, the cause does not arise;

because the cause does not arise, the fruit does not arise. This is called the characteristic of quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), as well as the characteristic of the extinction of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), and it is also called the characteristic of elimination (*apanayana-lakṣaṇa*). This constitutes the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths regarding arising and ceasing.

Regarding the wisdom of the Four Truths of Non-arising: one contemplates impure form and sees that the nature of form is inherently empty; it is not empty because form has been extinguished. It is like an image in a mirror, which lacks any reality.

To penetrate thoroughly that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are empty and non-existent, and to understand that suffering is without suffering yet possesses the True Reality—this is the wisdom of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

To know that the origin [of suffering] arises from the mind, and that the mind is like a magical illusion, so that the origin which arises is also like a magical illusion, and that all craving and views are equal to space—this is called the wisdom of the Truth of Origin (*samudaya-satya*).

The Path is fundamentally a collection of remedies; that which is remedied is already like an illusion or a transformation, and the remedy itself is also like an illusion or a transformation—this is called the wisdom of the Truth of the Path.

If a phenomenon were to arise, it could also cease; yet phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and thus do not now cease. If there were even a single phenomenon that transcended nirvana, I would likewise say it is like an illusion or a transformation—this is called the wisdom of the Truth of Cessation.
Although one knows that the five aggregates and sentient beings are like space, one vows to deliver these space-like sentient beings.
Although one knows that the accumulation [of suffering] is non-existent, one cuts off all deluded thoughts, as if fighting against space itself.
Although he knows that the nature of phenomena is non-dual, he diligently plants trees within emptiness.
Although there are no sentient beings who attain liberation, he brings immeasurable sentient beings to liberation.

Based on this, when one discusses the factors of enlightenment, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), and so forth as being true within the very phenomena themselves, this is called the wisdom of the four truths of non-arising (*anutpāda-catur-āryasatya-prajñā*).
Regarding the wisdom of the immeasurable four truths, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"If the Buddha’s teaching of the four truths were to encompass all phenomena exhaustively, then one should not say:"
"That which has not been spoken of is like the lands of the ten directions;
since the inclusion of all phenomena would not be exhaustive, there ought to be five truths.
The Buddha said:
"The Four Noble Truths encompass all; there is no fifth truth.
However, suffering has immeasurable aspects, and likewise, origination, cessation, and the path each have immeasurable aspects.
In that sutra, I did not speak of them at all."
"If it is emptiness, even emptiness itself lacks the nature of emptiness; how then could it be 'immeasurable'?
One should know that this refers to the wisdom of provisional differentiation.
This wisdom universally knows the distinctions between the provisional and the real within the ten dharma realms, and is thus called the wisdom of the Truth of Suffering."
Thoroughly knowing the differences among the afflictions of the five stages is the wisdom of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*);
thoroughly understanding the practices of the partial, the complete, the primary, and the auxiliary is the wisdom of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*);
and understanding the differences among the various gates of cessation within the sixteen aspects of the partial and complete [truths] is the wisdom of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The followers of the Two Vehicles merely take the medicine of the Four Noble Truths to treat the diseases of views and discursive thought; they emerge from birth and death for themselves and are proficient in making such distinctions.
The Bodhisattva acts as a Great King of Physicians, who must understand how to diagnose various pulses, recognize various diseases, master various medicines, and achieve various cures.

Based on this, one gives rise to various forms of compassion and performs various practices, including the perfections (*pāramitās*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), thereby maturing various sentient beings, purifying various Buddha-lands, and so forth, as extensively explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and other texts.
This is called the immeasurable wisdom of the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) wisdom of the Four Noble Truths: it is formed as four through the resolution and delusion of causes and conditions.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The jewel was upon his body, yet he cried out that it was lost; he wept in sorrow and lamentation.
He saw only his body and the wound, but did not see the jewel or the mirror."
"There is only sorrow and grief, with no further joy.
Thus, by being deluded regarding the path and cessation, one gives rise to suffering and its origin.
If one understands that the very substance of the wound is a precious jewel, then one rejoices rather than weeping.
By extinguishing ignorance, one immediately attains the blazing lamp of *sambodhi*.
This realization of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is itself the Path (*mārga*) and Cessation (*nirodha*).
The Path and Cessation are themselves Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its Accumulation (*samudaya*).
If suffering, its origin, and its cessation are themselves the path,
then the four truths would not be four.
Since the four are not four, the immeasurable is likewise not immeasurable.
Since the immeasurable is not [ultimately] immeasurable, then the provisional is not [ultimately] provisional;
because the provisional is not provisional, emptiness is not [ultimately] empty.

Not only is it that emptiness is non-empty, but the provisional is likewise non-provisional. When both are simultaneously transcended, one enters correctly; this is the simultaneous flow of quiescence and illumination.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the mark of quiescence.
To know all the various categories of practices and their characteristics is called the knowledge of all modes.
The characteristic of quiescent extinction (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*) is the simultaneous negation and simultaneous vanishing of both [extremes].
Knowing all aspects of the categories of practice is the simultaneous flow and simultaneous illumination.

When there is no deliberate mind to negate or illuminate, one rests spontaneously in quiescent knowing; therefore, it is called "inconceivable," which is precisely the wisdom of the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya-prajñā*).
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"There is no suffering and no truth of suffering, yet there is reality.
There is no origin, no path, and no cessation, nor are these truths, yet there is reality."
"Reality is itself the Middle Way, the Tathāgata, empty space, and Buddha-nature.
When one contemplates in this manner, through unconditional compassion, one uproots the suffering of the two extremes and bestows the bliss of the Middle Way."

Cultivating form as neither pure nor impure—that is emptiness, that is the provisional, that is the Middle; it is neither withered nor flourishing. Within this discourse on cessation, there is no factor of the path that is not fully perfected.
The universal relinquishing of the ten dharma-realms, both the support and the supported, is called *dāna* (giving);
reaching the other shore of *śīla* (precept) through the Middle Way and the precepts concomitant with the Path is called *śīla*;
abiding in the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*), unmoved by the two extremes, is called *kṣānti* (patience).
Being uninterrupted by the two extremes is called firm and vigorous diligence;
entering the King Samādhi and abiding in Śūraṅgama is called meditation;
and the Prajñā of the true mark is called wisdom.
Skillful application without deliberation is called "expedient means" (upāya);
mastery over the eight forms of self-mastery is called "power" (bala);
and the meditative concentration that transforms and emanates without conceptualization is called "vow" (praṇidhāna).
The three knowledges are termed "wisdom" when attained within a single moment of mind;
a single *pāramitā* is complete in ten, and likewise encompasses all Buddha-dharmas.

One practice contains infinite practices, and infinite practices are contained within one practice—this is the practice of the Tathāgata, and it is called the wisdom of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.
When cultivating this wisdom, one immediately abides in the stage of fearlessness, which is the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

One is freed from the five fears: namely, the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of rebirth in the evil realms, and the fear of being intimidated by great assemblies.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Do not fear greed, anger, or delusion.
When one is internally free from the three poisons and externally detached from the eight winds, then there is no fear of ill repute.
If one says, "I do not fear the hells," and so forth, then there is no fear of the evil realms;
if one says, "I do not fear śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas," then there is no fear of the great assembly;
and by seeing the Middle Way, there is no fear of the two kinds of death.
The wisdom of the true mark is eternally established, so there is no fear of not surviving.
Having attained entry into this stage, one possesses twenty-five samādhis, destroys the twenty-five states of existence, and manifests the self-nature within those twenty-five states of existence.
My nature is the true nature, and the true nature is the Buddha-nature.

By opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one awakens to the true Middle Way, severs the delusions of ignorance, and manifests the two bodies—the True and the Responsive. When conditions arise, the Responsive body immediately appears throughout the worlds of the hundred Buddhas, manifesting bodies within the ten Dharma realms and entering the ground of the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Thus, being able to benefit both oneself and others constitutes a truly great celebration; this is called the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This stage is endowed with four virtues:
destroying the afflictions of the twenty-five states of existence is called "purity";
destroying the karma of the twenty-five states of existence is called "self."
Not undergoing the twenty-five states of existence is called bliss;
the absence of birth and death within those twenty-five states is called permanence.
This is precisely the meaning of what is termed the manifestation of Buddha-nature as permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that one who is free from the five fears cultivates the wisdom of non-self; since the notion of a self does not arise, how could there be attachment to a self or attachment to the requisites of life?
This is the departure from the fear of lacking a livelihood;
having no desires or expectations toward others and constantly benefiting all sentient beings, this is the departure from the fear of ill repute;
and not giving rise to the view of self or the conception of a self within the mind, this is the departure from the fear of death.
When this life ends, one will certainly meet with Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in future worlds; this is the removal of the fear of the evil realms.
Contemplating that there is no one equal in the world, much less superior, is the removal of the fear of the great assembly.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* is likewise.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains:
"Among these, the first is based on the body;..."
The second depends on speech;
the third and fourth depend on the body;
the fifth depends on the mind.
"Living" (*jīvita*) refers to the various requisites used by the body that can support life; thus, they are called "means of livelihood" (*ājīva*), for life is what is sustained.
This is a case of speaking of the effect within the context of its cause; the Bodhisattva has no such fear regarding this.
Furthermore, names and verbal expressions all depend on the faults of speech.
To protect one's name without seeking gain or support, and with a mind that does not hope for the respect of others, is called being "without ill repute."
The fifth [point] can be understood based on the mind.
The third and fourth are based on the body.
Because one has no attachment to the good path and no aversion toward the evil path, and because the body itself is free from attachment and aversion, there is no fear of the evil paths.
Furthermore, because one neither loves nor hates the body, there is no fear of death.
I privately maintain that by not fearing desire and the like, there is no accumulation of karma through volitional action (*abhisamskāra*).
Not fearing the evil realms is called the non-actuated destruction of suffering.
Not fearing the great assembly is the non-actuated establishment of the Path.
Having no fear of lack of livelihood and no fear of death is the seeing of the nature and attainment of permanence; it is the non-actuated establishment of cessation.
Furthermore, by destroying the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), one destroys that which can contain the fruit.
Because the states of existence are destroyed, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is subverted;
because the fruit is destroyed, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is subverted.
The attainment of the twenty-five samādhis establishes the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).

Seeing that the twenty-five [elements] possess the nature of self (*ātman*), and that this nature of self is itself the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), establishes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
To destroy the twenty-five states of existence is to be free from afflictions; this is the virtue of purity.
To destroy the twenty-five states of existence is to be free from suffering as a result; this is the virtue of permanence.
To attain the twenty-five samādhis is bliss.
Seeing that the nature of the twenty-five principles is the Self, the four virtues are manifest.
Now, the names of the twenty-five samādhis will be explained according to the intent of the four *siddhāntas*:
first, they are established according to the occasion and the inclination [of the practitioner].
It is like a man who has many sons and gives each a distinct name so that the brothers do not become confused.

The twenty-five samādhis are likewise; by citing a specific name for each, one ensures that conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is not disordered—how could one possibly hold to them with fixed attachment?
Second, according to the convenience of their respective meanings, each is established with a name based on its underlying reason.
Third, according to the correspondence of specific matters, each has its own primary function; they are named according to what they counteract.
Fourth, although in reality there are no names, characters are established based on principle.
Although there are four intentions, the twenty-five samādhis are mostly established by means of antidotes and in accordance with principle.
The general explanation of the twenty-five [categories] each consists of four points:
first, to set forth the faults and afflictions of the various realms of existence;
second, to clarify the merits of the fundamental dharma.
Third, completing the practice by attaining samādhi;
fourth, destroying existence through compassion.
Each and every one is thus.

Regarding the statement that the existence of hell is destroyed by means of the stainless samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*): hell is the place for the retribution of heavy defilements, and the causes of such retribution are themselves defilements—namely, the defilement of evil karma, the defilement of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), the defilement of *rajas* (dust-like passions), and the defilement of ignorance (*avidyā*). These constitute the first [category].
The Bodhisattva first perceives these faults and, in order to destroy all defilements, cultivates the fundamental precepts previously elucidated to destroy the defilement of evil karma;
cultivates the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and other concentrations previously elucidated to subdue the defilements of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);
and cultivates the wisdom of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing previously elucidated to destroy the defilements of views and thoughts.
Second: Cultivating the immeasurable wisdom previously elucidated, one destroys the defilement of dust-like sands;
cultivating the unconditioned wisdom previously elucidated, one destroys the defilement of ignorance.
By destroying the defilements of views and afflictions, the samādhi of ultimate truth is accomplished;
by destroying the defilements of evil karma and the dust-like defilements, the samādhi of conventional truth is accomplished;
and by destroying the defilement of ignorance, the sovereign samādhi of the Middle Way is accomplished—thus completing these three.
When the Bodhisattva personally shatters the various defilements of the hells, every phrase contains vows of compassion that permeate the Dharma-realm in secret.

If there are sentient beings within those hells who possess the karmic conditions related to compassion, the Bodhisattva responds to them through the power of the King Samādhi; while the nature of reality remains unmoving, he is able to manifest in accordance with their needs.
Just as with Vasu and Devadatta, he manifests bodies appropriate to them and teaches the Dharma appropriate to them.
If there is the potential for goodness within that hell, he responds with compassion through the practice of precepts, causing them to leave suffering and attain happiness;
if there is the potential for entering emptiness, he responds with compassion through the wisdom of birth and non-birth, causing them to realize the ultimate truth.
For those with the capacity to enter the provisional, he responds with immeasurable wisdom and compassion to enable them to attain conventional truth;
for those with the capacity to enter the Middle Way, he responds with unconditioned wisdom and compassion to enable them to attain the King Samādhi.

Having first been stainless oneself, one now causes others to be stainless; therefore, this samādhi is named "Stainless. The subsequent sections follow this same pattern, so they will not be recorded in detail hereafter.

Regarding the existence of animals, that which is destroyed by the *apratihata-samādhi* (non-retrogression samādhi) refers to the fact that animals lack shame and remorse and thus fall away from the wholesome path. This falling away is due to evil karma, due to the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), due to the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*), and due to ignorance (*avidyā*).
To destroy all forms of regression, the Bodhisattva cultivates the previously mentioned precepts to overcome regression caused by evil karma;

he cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to subdue regression caused by views and afflictions (*kleśa*); he cultivates the wisdom of birthlessness to overcome regression caused by views and afflictions;
and he cultivates immeasurable wisdom to overcome regression caused by the dust-like and sand-like delusions.
By cultivating non-active wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-prajñā*), one destroys the regression caused by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are destroyed, one attains non-regression in status, and the samādhi of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is perfected.
Because the dust-like sands of evil karma are destroyed, one attains non-regression in practice, and the samādhi of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is perfected.
Because ignorance is destroyed, one attains non-retrogressive mindfulness and accomplishes the samādhi of the Middle Way.
All the various practices originally cultivated were accompanied by vows of compassion, which secretly permeate the Dharma-realm.

Among those in the realm of animals, if there are karmic conditions related to compassion, he responds to them by means of the power of the King Samādhi, without wavering from the nature of reality (dharmatā).
One should manifest whatever body is appropriate and preach whatever Dharma is appropriate—whether as a dragon, an elephant, a partridge, or a great vulture.
If there is the potential for goodness, one should respond with the compassion of precepts and meditative concentration to cause them to leave suffering and attain happiness;

if there is the potential for entering emptiness, one should respond with the compassion of the wisdom of birth and non-birth to cause them to leave existence and attain non-existence, thereby perfecting the samādhi of ultimate truth.

For those with the capacity to enter the provisional, one responds with immeasurable wisdom, compassion, and skillful means, enabling them to avoid falling into emptiness and attain the provisional; thus, the samādhi of the conventional truth is accomplished.

For those with the capacity to enter the middle, one responds with non-conceptual wisdom, compassion, and skillful means, enabling them to transcend extremes and enter the middle; thus, the royal samādhi is accomplished.
Because the Bodhisattva himself does not regress and causes others not to regress, it is called the Samādhi of Non-regression.

Regarding the hungry ghosts who possess the "Samādhi of Delighting in Mental Application" yet destroy it: they possess the suffering of the evil karma of constant hunger and thirst; the suffering of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the suffering of adventitious darkness and obstructions; and the fundamental suffering of ignorance (*avidyā*).
To destroy all sufferings, the Bodhisattva cultivates the aforementioned observance of precepts to destroy the suffering of evil karma;
he cultivates meditative concentration to subdue the suffering of views and afflictions;
and he cultivates the wisdom of birthlessness to destroy the suffering of views and afflictions.
Cultivating immeasurable wisdom breaks the suffering as numerous as dust motes;
cultivating unconditioned wisdom breaks the suffering of ignorance.
By breaking the suffering of views and thoughts, the samādhi of the bliss of the unconditioned mind is accomplished.
One destroys the dust and sands of evil karma and suffering; through extensive learning and discernment, one accomplishes the Samādhi of Joy.
One destroys the suffering of ignorance; through constancy and joy, one accomplishes Samādhi.
By means of the original practice of compassion, one silently permeates the Dharma-realm.

In that realm of hungry ghosts, if there are those with the karmic conditions who are connected to compassion, the King, through the power of samādhi, responds to them without wavering from the nature of reality (dharmatā), manifesting a body appropriate for them and teaching the Dharma appropriate for them.

If there are those with the capacity for goodness, one responds to them with compassion through the observance of precepts, causing fragrant milk to flow from one's hands to provide them with full satisfaction;
if there are those with the capacity to enter emptiness, one responds to them with the compassion that gives rise to non-arising, causing them to reach the shore of the unconditioned;
if there are those with the capacity to enter the provisional, one responds to them with immeasurable compassion, causing them to sport within the five realms of existence.

For those with the capacity to enter [this state], one responds with non-conceptual compassion (*nirnimitta-karuṇā*), causing them to purify the roots of the three poisons and attain the Buddha-way without doubt.
Since the Bodhisattva has personally attained bliss and further enables others to attain bliss, it is therefore called the Samādhi of Mental Bliss (*cittasukha-samādhi*).

Regarding the existence of asuras who employ the Samādhi of Joy: because asuras are generally full of suspicion and fear, they possess the suspicion and fear of evil karma, the suspicion and fear of views and afflictions, the suspicion and fear of the sands of dust [of phenomena], and the suspicion and fear of ignorance.
The Bodhisattva cultivates various practices in order to shatter these doubts and fears:
by observing the precepts, he shatters the doubts and fears regarding evil karma;
by cultivating the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), he subdues the fears of views and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Cultivating the wisdom born of non-arising destroys the fear of views and afflictions;
cultivating immeasurable wisdom destroys the fear of dust-like [delusions];
cultivating the wisdom of non-action destroys the fear of ignorance.
Because the views and afflictions are destroyed, the Samādhi of Emptiness and Dharma-Joy is accomplished;
because the dust-like sands of evil karma are destroyed, the Samādhi of Being Seen with Joy by All Sentient Beings is accomplished;
and because ignorance is destroyed, the Samādhi of the King of Joy is accomplished.
By means of their original practices, compassion, and vows, they secretly permeate the Dharma-realm.

Within that realm of asuras, if there are those with the karmic conditions related to compassion, they respond to them by the power of the King Samādhi—without wavering from the nature of reality—manifesting appropriate bodies and preaching appropriate teachings.
For those with the capacity for the wholesome expedient means, one should employ the compassion of the precept-observing body to cause them to leave behind the fear of evil karma;
for those with the capacity to enter emptiness, one should employ the compassion of the arising of non-arising to cause them to leave behind the fear of views and afflictions;
for those with the capacity to enter the provisional, one should employ immeasurable compassion to cause them to leave behind the fear of ignorance.
For those with the capacity to enter this [state], one should employ non-conceptual compassion to cause them to leave behind the fear of ignorance.
By personally realizing the three joys and causing others to no longer have the three fears, it is therefore called the Samādhi of Joyful Delight.
All the names used previously were established based on their respective antidotes.
As for the existence of Pūrvavideha, which is destroyed by the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi*, it is merely named according to the circumstance that the sun rises in the east at dawn.

The sun is like the light of wisdom, capable of illuminating and dispelling delusion; yet the people of the eastern continent possess the darkness of evil karma, the darkness of views and afflictions, the darkness of dust-like defilements, and the darkness of ignorance.
In order to illuminate these various darknesses, the bodhisattva cultivates the light of the aforementioned precepts to shatter the darkness of evil karma;
cultivates the flowing light of meditative concentration to subdue the darkness of views and afflictions;
and cultivates the light of all-knowledge to destroy the darkness of views and afflictions.
Cultivating the light of the knowledge of the paths, one destroys the darkness of the sands of dust;
cultivating the light of the knowledge of all modes, one destroys the darkness of ignorance.
Because the darkness of views and afflictions is destroyed, the samādhi of the sun-like light of all-knowledge is accomplished.
Because the darkness of the sands of dust is destroyed, the Sunlight Samādhi of the Knowledge of the Paths is accomplished;
because the darkness of ignorance is destroyed, the Sunlight Samādhi of the Knowledge of All Modes is accomplished.
By means of the compassionate vows made through his original practice, he silently permeates the Dharma-realm.

If there are those in Pūrvavideha who possess the karmic conditions related to compassion, the King, through the power of samādhi, responds to them by manifesting his body and preaching the Dharma, without wavering from the nature of reality (dharmatā).
If there is a capacity for wholesome phenomena, one responds with the compassion of upholding the precepts, causing them to escape the darkness of evil karma;
if there is a capacity for entering emptiness, one responds with the compassion of the non-arising of birth, causing them to escape the darkness of views and afflictions;
if there is a capacity for entering the provisional, one responds with immeasurable compassion, causing them to escape the darkness of ignorance.
For those with the capacity to enter [this state], one responds with non-conceptual compassion to enable them to escape the darkness of ignorance.
Having personally shattered the darkness, one also causes others to shatter it; therefore, this is called the Sunlight Samādhi.

Regarding the existence [of the moon] in Aparagoyānī and its destruction by the *candraprabhā-samādhi*: when the moon first appears in the west on a moonlit night, it is likewise given a name according to its immediate circumstances.
The moon also illuminates darkness; this is analogous to the light of the sun, and so forth.

Regarding the use of the Heat-Flame Samādhi to destroy Uttarakuru: the northern region is a land of darkness where ice freezes and is difficult to melt; were it not for the blazing illumination of the heat-flame, it would never be fused and refined.
The people of the northern continent cling to the notion of self and are difficult to transform and deliver;
unless they possess the fire of wisdom and the flames of insight to eliminate the mind of "mine-ness," they will ultimately not attain liberation.

That they are "without mine" is itself a false conceptualization; for there still remains the self-nature of the person-self (*pudgala-ātman*), the dharma-self (*dharma-ātman*), and the suchness-self (*tathatā-ātman*).
To destroy these various selves, the bodhisattva cultivates the wisdom of arising-and-ceasing as well as non-arising-and-non-ceasing to destroy the self-nature of the person-self;
he cultivates immeasurable wisdom to destroy the dharma-self.
By cultivating non-conceptual wisdom, one shatters the self of *tathatā*.
Attaining the emptiness of persons, one perfects the flame of wisdom regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*);
attaining the emptiness of phenomena, one perfects the flame of wisdom regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Attaining the emptiness of *tathatā*, one perfects the flaming wisdom of the Middle Way.
Through primordial compassion, one silently permeates the *dharmadhātu*.

If there are those in Uttarakuru with the karmic conditions to respond to this compassion, by the power of the King Samādhi, without wavering from the *dharmatā*, one goes to meet them, manifesting a body and preaching the Dharma.
For those with the capacity for goodness, one should respond with the compassion of precepts to cause them to avoid the false calculation of a non-existent self;
for those with the capacity to enter emptiness, one should respond with the compassion of arising and non-arising to cause them to avoid the self of intrinsic nature;
for those with the capacity to enter the provisional, one should respond with immeasurable compassion to cause them to avoid the self of dharmas.
For those with the capacity to enter [this stage], one responds with non-conceptual compassion (*nirnimitta-karuṇā*), causing them to avoid the self of *tathatā*.
By personally destroying the false self and causing others to destroy the false self, it is therefore called the *marīci-samādhi* (the samādhi of the mirage).

That which exists in Jambudvīpa is destroyed by the illusion-like samādhi; for in the southern continent, karmic retributions are manifold and lifespans are indefinite, being just like magical illusions.
This is karma produced as an illusion from the mind, producing illusory views and afflictions, producing illusory ignorance, and producing illusory nescience.
To shatter these illusions, the Bodhisattva relies on the observance of precepts to produce the illusory state of non-action, thereby destroying the illusion of fetters and karma;
and by relying on meditative concentration, they produce the illusory state of the liberations.
From the wisdom of birthlessness arises the illusory manifestation of the outflow-free;
from immeasurable wisdom arises the illusory manifestation of the outflowing;
from the wisdom of non-action arises the illusory manifestation of that which is neither outflowing nor outflow-free.
When the illusion of view-and-thought is shattered, the illusion of the ultimate truth is realized;
when the illusion of ignorance is shattered, the illusion of the conventional truth is realized;
when the illusion of nescience is shattered, the illusion of the Middle Way is realized.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata is a great master of illusion.

In that Jambudvīpa, there are various karmic conditions related to his vows; through his original compassion, he responds to them according to their capacity, personally dissolving his own illusions while manifesting illusions for others. For this reason, it is called the Illusion-like Samādhi (māyopama-samādhi).
The rest is as explained above.

Regarding the four heavenly kings (*cāturmahārājika*), those who use the Immovable Samādhi (*āniñjya-samādhi*) to destroy [defilements] are celestial beings who protect the lands and traverse the worlds; thus, they possess the movement of karmic retribution, as well as the movements of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-vitarka*), the dust-and-sand-like afflictions (*rajas-śata*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
When a bodhisattva cultivates various practices, they shatter all fluctuations and accomplish samādhi.

Through the permeation of vows and the resonance of karmic conditions, by means of original compassion, they cause others to break the four fluctuations and achieve the three immovables; therefore, it is called the Immovable Samādhi.
The details are as explained above.

Regarding the existence of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and the use of the Samādhi Difficult to Subdue (*durjayā-samādhi*): this is the pinnacle of the earth-dwelling heavens; it is the "difficult to subdue" of karmic retribution, namely, the difficulty of subduing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
When a bodhisattva cultivates various practices and excels therein, they overcome all that is difficult to subdue and personally attain samādhi.
Through their vows, they influence others;
if there is a karmic affinity, they employ their original compassion to enable others to realize it as well. For this reason, this samādhi is named "Difficult to Subdue" (Durnivāra).
The rest is as explained above.

As for the existence of the Yāma Heaven, those who destroy [afflictions] by means of the Samādhi of Delight find their joy therein; this celestial realm is empty of swords and staves, and they take this very absence of combat to be their delight.

This is the joy found within the realm of karmic retribution, yet it does not include the joy of immovable karma, nor the joy of the untainted, the knowledge of the modes of the path, or the intermediate wisdoms.
The Bodhisattva cultivates various practices in order to destroy all forms of dissatisfaction, thereby personally attaining the Samādhi of the Joyful Mind of the Three Truths.
He vows to permeate the Dharma-realm.
For those with the karmic conditions, he causes their minds to rejoice through his original compassion; therefore, this samādhi is named "Delighting the Mind.
The rest is as explained above.
Regarding the Tuṣita Heaven, there are those who destroy [defilements] by means of the blue-colored samādhi.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"The karmic retribution of this heaven is blue; its palaces, garments, ornaments, and all else are entirely blue."

The Bodhisattva, in order to destroy all notions of blue, cultivates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). While the ultimate truth is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white, it perceives blue, yellow, red, and white.
The ultimate truth is neither morality, concentration, nor wisdom, yet it is morality, concentration, and wisdom.
By means of the precepts, one breaks the blue of karmic retribution;
by means of the wisdom of non-arising, one breaks the blue of views and afflictions.
It is likewise with not seeing the true as true, not seeing the false as false, and not seeing the middle as middle.
When the three blue obstructions are destroyed, one spontaneously achieves the three truths and the three blue samādhis.
This extends to the achievement of the samādhis of others through resonance, which may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

The yellow samādhi destroys existence in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; the red samādhi destroys existence in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and the white samādhi destroys existence in the First Dhyāna—all of which are karmic retributions.
The examples for white and other colors follow the same principle as the samādhi of blue; the general meaning can thus be understood.

Regarding the samādhi of white: in the first dhyāna, being free from the five desires constitutes "white," yet because one has not yet abandoned applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is also "black."
