The "black" consists of the afflictions of view and thought, the dust-like afflictions, and ignorance; by destroying these various forms of black and cultivating the "white" of all practices, one spontaneously achieves samādhi for oneself and, as explained above, brings about samādhi for others.

Regarding "various samādhis shatter the existence of the Brahma King": the Brahma King presides over a great trichiliocosm; since his species are manifold, this constitutes various karmic retributions.
Yet he has not yet perceived the various emptinesses, the various conventionalities, or the various middle ways.
Having destroyed these various [defilements], one cultivates various practices;
one accomplishes various things for oneself and also accomplishes various things for others,
as explained above.

Regarding the second dhyāna, which employs the "pair samādhi": the second dhyāna uniquely possesses the two factors of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) and joy (*prīti*); the remaining factors are shared with other dhyānas. This constitutes the "pair of fruition."
Yet they have not yet seen the dual emptiness, the dual provisionality, and the dual middle.

As explained above, regarding the third dhyāna, the practitioner employs the Thunder-Sound Samādhi; this dhyānic bliss is most profound, like fish in ice or hibernating insects. This is an attachment to the bliss of karmic fruition, as well as an attachment to the bliss of emptiness, the bliss of provisionality, and the bliss of the middle.
To startle all pleasures, one cultivates the practice of the sound of thunder.
The remainder is as explained above.
Regarding the fourth dhyāna, the use of the *Vṛṣṭisamaya* (Rain-Pouring) samādhi: the fourth dhyāna is like the great earth, possessing all kinds of seeds.
If rain does not fall, the sprout cannot grow.
All roots of goodness reside within the four dhyānas—namely, the seeds of karma and the seeds of the three truths.
By practicing the rain of various deeds, samādhi arises spontaneously.
"Compassion responds to capacities, giving rise to the samādhis of others," and so forth.

Regarding the existence of the "samādhi like empty space" in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), non-Buddhists falsely reckon that *nirvāṇa* is not empty; they claim that karmic retribution is not empty and that all three truths are not void.
By cultivating various practices of emptiness and purity, one accomplishes both oneself and others, and so forth.
As for the Anāgāmin heaven, they employ the Mirror-like Samādhi.
Although these noble, untainted devas attain pure form, it is merely a pure form resulting from karmic retribution.
Not yet having fully investigated the emptiness of form is like a mirror that has not reached ultimate clarity;
not yet knowing that form is provisional is like a mirror in which no image has appeared;
not yet knowing within form is like not yet having attained the full perfection of the mirror.
The rest is as explained above.

Regarding the station of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one who employs the samādhi of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*) attains liberation from the "cage of form" (*rūpa-kośa*); this is the non-obstruction of karmic fruition (*vipāka*), but it is not yet the non-obstruction of the Middle Way consisting of emptiness, the conventional, and the middle.
The rest is as explained above.

Regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), "using the samādhi of permanence" means that this meditative concentration takes the uninterrupted continuity of consciousness as its permanence; this is the fruit of retribution from that concentration, not the permanence of the three unconditioned states, nor the permanence of transformative function, nor the permanence of bliss.
For example, as stated above and so forth.

Regarding the station of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), that which is destroyed by the bliss of samādhi is, in this state, like delusion (*moha*); because it is delusion, it is suffering, and thus even ignorance (*avidyā*) is suffering.
For example, as stated above and so forth:

regarding the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one who employs my samādhi to break through it perceives the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the fruit of nirvāṇa; yet there still exist subtle afflictions and a lack of mastery, even unto the lack of mastery over ignorance (*avidyā*).
Through cultivation, one breaks through [delusions] to attain the true self, the conventional self, and the self of permanence, bliss, and purity—
as explained extensively above.
These twenty-five are all termed *samādhi*, which refers to the rectification and stabilization of the mind.
In the True Dharma (Satyasiddhi), emptiness and the outflow-free (anāsrava) are taken as rectification;
in the emergence from the conventional (prajñapti), responding to the capacities of beings is taken as rectification;
and in the Middle Way, the negation of the two extremes is taken as rectification.
Therefore, as all [states] fully possess the three truths, they are collectively termed *samādhi*.

Furthermore, regarding the title "King": when emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*) are harmonized and rectified, one has not yet attained the status of a King; thus, while those of the Two Vehicles enter into emptiness and Bodhisattvas emerge into the provisional, they are not called Dharma Kings.
Because the Middle Way is balanced and upright, it is entitled "King.
Each and every samādhi possesses this Middle Way, and thus each is called a "King.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
“The twenty-five samādhis are called the Kings of All Samādhis” refers to the meaning of their high status;
“If one enters these samādhis, all samādhis enter therein” refers to the meaning of the vastness of their essence;
“They respond to the twenty-five types of sentient beings” refers to the length of their function.
Within the stage of fearlessness, one fully attains the various powers and functions of twenty-five samādhis:
Mount Sumeru may enter a mustard seed without harming the trees;
the ocean may be contained within a pore without distressing the turtles and fish.
Although dwelling in hell, their body and mind experience no suffering.
Their transformations and manifestations appear and disappear; they reach afar without moving. This is precisely the profound meaning.
It is because the practice of wisdom and holiness has been perfected that such power can be possessed.
Question:
"Samādhi destroys existence" is a passage from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; how can this [text] be explained by it?
Answer:
The third [verse] says:
"The Dharma King who destroys existence appears in the world, preaching the Dharma according to the desires of sentient beings.
The four meanings are clearly expressed and fully present therein.

Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that the bodhisattva destroys existence (*bhava*), while this sutra clarifies that the Dharma King destroys existence; thus, its meaning is made even more manifest.
The explanation of the Noble Practices (*āryacaryā*) is concluded.
Second, regarding the "Brahma-practitioner" (*brahmacarya*): "Brahma" means purity.
To realize the attainment of liberation through the witnessing of freedom from the two extremes of craving is called purity.
To bestow this pure dharma upon sentient beings is precisely non-referential loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
When a Bodhisattva cultivates the noble practices with the mind of Great Nirvana, they attain the stage of fearlessness and possess the twenty-five samādhis and their boundless great functions.

At that time, compassion is true Brahma-conduct; it is not the four immeasurable minds cultivated by other Brahma-heaven deities, nor is it the compassion based on sentient beings or phenomena found in the Tripiṭaka or the Shared Teaching.
By now cultivating all practices through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"If someone should ask: [text continues]"
Who is the root of all virtues?
One should say:
it is loving-kindness (maitrī).
Since loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the very foundation of practice, it is called "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*).
If one follows the terminology of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanju*), it is as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*:
"Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata; loving-kindness is Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*)."
If compassion is not endowed with the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the thirty-two marks, it is the compassion of a śrāvaka;
if it is fully endowed with these, it is the compassion of a Tathāgata.
This loving-kindness is itself the great mass of Dharma;
this loving-kindness is itself Great Nirvana.
The power of loving-kindness is vast and profound, and as it is endowed with all adornments of merit and virtue, it is called the Brahma-faring.
Third, regarding the "heavenly practice" (*devayāna*): the ultimate heaven is the principle of naturalness; this refers to the stage prior to the Path.
Because practice is established by means of this principle, this refers to the stage during the Path.
Because the principle is manifested through practice, this refers to the stage subsequent to the Path.
Now, because practice is established by means of principle, it is called "heavenly practice" (devayāna).
Although a bodhisattva has entered the first stage (bhūmi), they should not abide in that first stage, for to do so would constitute a state of grasping at attainments.

Cultivating the wisdom of the ten higher stages involves ten successive instances of generating true cultivated wisdom; because practice is established through principle, it is called "celestial conduct" (devayāna).
This celestial conduct is precisely the adornment of wisdom.
Because they seek the Buddha-way above, there are the holy practice and the celestial practice;
because they transform sentient beings below, there are the Brahma practice, the sick practice, and the infant practice.
Regarding the fourth stage, the "Infant Practitioner": as their merit and wisdom further increase, the true nature (*dharmatā*) becomes increasingly manifest.
Although they do not intentionally apply effort to benefit sentient beings, they spontaneously possess both hidden and manifest benefits for them.
The power of heavenly conduct provides hidden benefit, while the power of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) provides manifest benefit.
Although sentient beings possess the potential for minor wholesome roots, they cannot grow or flourish without being awakened by a bodhisattva.

The power of the roots of goodness of charity is like a magnet attracting iron; by blending its light with beneficial conduct, it enables sentient beings to behold the Bodhisattva and join him at the beginning of his training.
Gradually cultivating the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions leads to the retributive fruits of the human and celestial realms; such practices are like the conduct of a young sapling.

Furthermore, the teaching of the two hundred and fifty precepts, as well as the contemplation, refinement, perfuming, and cultivation, along with the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment, are all the "infant-like" practices of the Two Vehicles.

Furthermore, he manifested the practice of the six pāramitās over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the cultivation of the marks and signs over a hundred kalpas, and the minor virtuous deeds of a bodhisattva who subdues afflictions through the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, it demonstrates that "form is identical to emptiness," being without arising or ceasing, corresponding to the practices of minor goodness in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

It also demonstrates that they correspond to the distinct stages and sequential progression of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), as well as the minor practices of goodness within the semblance Middle Way.

All of this is through the power of a compassionate mind, which stoops to the level of the common and small, uplifting and guiding them to fulfillment. From this compassionate bestowal of joy, one initiates the conduct of an infant.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"One can utter great words, namely 'Bha' and 'Ho. This refers to seeking Buddhahood through the minor practices of the six perfections; therefore, they are called "great words."
Furthermore, it says:

"Not perceiving such characteristics as day and night, or intimacy and distance," which is identical to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), meaning that form itself is emptiness (*rūpam eva śūnyatā*).
It further says:

"Being unable to perform great or small matters"—where "great matters" refers to the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and "small matters" refers to the mind of the Two Vehicles—this corresponds to the Distinct Teaching (*bhinnadeśanā*).
The Separate Teaching (biejiao) is not samsara, and thus there are no five heinous offenses;
it is not nirvana, and thus there is no Hinayana mind.
It further states:
"The yellowing leaves of the willow tree" refers to the five precepts and ten wholesome acts of humans and devas, who are like infants.
It is also said:
"That which is not the Way is treated as the Way, because it can produce subtle causes and conditions for the Way."
This is equivalent to the infant of the Two Vehicles.

Through the power of the roots of goodness of compassion, one is able to emerge from the provisional to transform sentient beings; this is equivalent to the skillful means of minor good, which leads others into the Buddha-wisdom, thereby becoming the infant of the Perfect Teaching.
The Sūtra says:
"It cannot arise or abide, come or go, or speak.
As the Sūtra says, and so forth.
Furthermore, the distinctions between the coarse and the sublime, and the opening up of the coarse to reveal the sublime, may be understood through similar examples, as explained at length.
Fifth, regarding the practitioner’s illness, this arises from unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*).
If one initially gives rise to even a small amount of goodness, there will necessarily be "sick conduct.
Now, when it arises alongside goodness, it is called "infant conduct";
when it arises alongside afflictions, it is called "sick conduct."
Because the illnesses of sentient beings permeate my heart with great compassion, I am thus ill.

At times I sport within the hells, or take the form of an animal, or manifest as a hungry ghost and so forth; all these are identical to the illness of evil karma, such as that of Devadatta and others.

Furthermore, he manifests having parents, a wife, and children; [enduring] golden spikes and horse-barley; seeking clothing against the cold wind; and seeking milk for a fever—these demonstrate that humans and devas possess the afflictions of fetters, karma, birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that at the site of enlightenment, the thirty-four moments of mind sever the fetters; he shows that these are identical to the maladies of view and thought characteristic of the Two Vehicles, employing skillful means to draw them near and instructing them to apply themselves with diligence.
The Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teachings are also like this.

Furthermore, they share with the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching the site of the terrace of tranquility and extinction, where they first sever the afflictions of the sands and the ignorance of non-enlightenment.
Therefore, these Bodhisattvas, being identical to those afflictions, pervade the Dharma-realm to benefit sentient beings.
The five successive practices are now complete.
Question:
The Noble Practice realizes three stages, and the Brahma Practice realizes two stages; why do the Celestial Practice, the Illness Practice, and the Infant Practice not realize any stages?
Answer:

The two practices of the Noble Ones (ārya) and Brahmā are called the causes of cultivation; therefore, the treatise discusses their realization. The practice of the gods (deva) is precisely that which is realized.
As for the two practices of the sick and the child, they arise as responses from the fruit; therefore, they are not discussed in terms of realization.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
the Sūtra reveals the meaning of distinct stages, wherein those prior to the grounds each enter into realization individually;
the Sūtra reveals the meaning of perfection, wherein upon reaching the grounds, one enters into realization as a single unity.

Furthermore, it is not that those prior to the stages do not cultivate the perfect [path], nor is it that there are no distinctions upon reaching the stages. These are presented reciprocally to facilitate understanding, so as not to burden the text with redundancy.
Regarding the distinctions prior to the stages: through the practice of ethical discipline progressing from shallow to deep, one realizes the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*);
through the practice of meditative concentration progressing from shallow to deep, one realizes the Stage of Endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
The practice of wisdom proceeds from the shallow to the profound, realizing the stage of fearlessness (*abhaya-bhūmi*).
As for those who proceed together upon the stages (*bhūmi*), how could there be three stages that are entirely and eternally distinct?
It is simply that at the moment of ascending the stages, one is not moved by the two extremes; thus it is called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Upholding the Buddha-dharma above and bearing the burden of sentient beings below is called the Stage of Endurance;
attaining mastery over both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is called the Stage of Fearlessness.
The Ground of Fearlessness is named after the virtue of self;
the Ground of Patience is named after the virtue of joy;
the Ground of Immovability is named after the virtue of constancy.
The virtue of purity permeates all three stages.

On the day one ascends the stages (*bhūmi*), the four virtues are simultaneously perfected, remaining without increase or decrease; this is simply because such is the nature of the path of transformation.
It is, for example, like the principle of "three in the morning and four in the evening."
From the stage of "Leaving the Ground" onwards, each ground has its own practice and each ground has its own realization.

This self-practice is simply the cultivation of the heavenly practices (*deva-caryā*), and this self-realization is simply the realization of the heavenly practices; therefore, the realization of the heavenly practices is not explained separately.
If one transforms others prior to the stages (bhūmi), it is called the "Brahma-conduct" (brahmacarya).
Loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy are the activities for transforming others; practicing the stage of the "only-child" is its realization.
Equanimity is the principle-practice for transforming others; the equality of emptiness is its realization.
These two stages are not entirely distinct; because one ascends to the stages through compassion, they speak of the "only child";
and because compassion is identical to the essence [of reality], they speak of "emptiness and equality."
In each stage there is compassion shared with those who are evil, which is called the practice of the sick;
in each stage there is loving-kindness shared with those who are good, which is called the practice of the infant.
Since the realization of the Path is the same, it is not explained separately.
The merits of the Buddha-ground can only be approached through reverent faith; how could one possibly attempt to definitively discern them with a mind shrouded in darkness?
A brief response is thus provided, and so forth.
